what_it_does: When a computer multiplies two matrices where most entries are zero (called sparse matrix multiplication), the chip keeps pulling data from slow off-chip memory (the large storage chips outside the processor) because its small, fast on-chip memory — think of it as a scratchpad — cannot efficiently hold both matrices at once. Avalanche is a hardware design that applies three coordinated tricks to fix this: it reorders the columns of one matrix so that the data the chip needs next is already sitting in the scratchpad; it immediately throws away partial results as soon as they are finished rather than letting them linger and crowd out useful data; and it keeps the matrix entries that will be reused soon at the front of the queue when deciding what to evict from the scratchpad. Together, these techniques let Avalanche keep both matrices on-chip in a chip area of about 6 square millimeters, dramatically cutting the number of expensive trips to slow off-chip memory.
